speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head S of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The workforce profile in Singapore is changing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Since April 2017, we have the new Employment Claims Tribunal (ECT) as well as the Tripartite Alliance for Disputes Management (TADM) to assist PMEs to a speedier resolution of their disputes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Employment Claims Tribunal, which came into force on 1 April 2017, has already done away with a salary cap for salary-related claims by employees but the ECT is limited to salary-related claims, both contractually and statutorily.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The median gross monthly salaries of workers stand at $4,056 in 2016.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For PMETs, the gross monthly salaries for P-50 – or at the 50th percentile – for residents stand at $5,910 as at June 2016.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our Labour Movement has also been challenged with difficult questions concerning various parts of the EA the past few years as it also affects our unions and union members amidst a backdrop of a higher number of layoffs in 2016, unfair dismissals, mergers, acquisitions, outsourcing, volatility and interesting new vehicles involving the sale and transfer of companies/staff.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Based on cases our Labour Movement has encountered in the past few years, a changing workforce profile, upward movements of median wages as well as a stronger impetus to ensure our employment laws stay relevant, I hope to see three things.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Despite the last round of EA amendments in April 2014, we have still been receiving feedback/queries from PMEs through various channels, such as through our unions/union leaders, TADM, my Meet-the-People sessions (MPS), our U PME Centres, our National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) LawWorks Legal Clinics, as well as through my social media platforms such as LinkedIn and Facebook, from aggrieved PMEs whom we were unable to assist as they earned more than $4,500 per month.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Despite the amendments to the Industrial Relations Act (IRA) in April 2015 to allow collective representation of PMEs by all unions, in some of our unionised companies, management have occasionally attempted to use this "$4,500 limit” in the EA as a proxy to suggest that the union cannot expand its scope of representation beyond those earning more than this sum.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With rising median wages, including that of PMEs, and PMEs gradually forming the majority of the workforce, there is a need to review this $4,500 cap to ensure the EA serves the majority of the working population.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the intent of the cap is to strike a balance between the rights of employees and to allow companies to manage their labour obligations and costs, the changing profile of our workforce requires a regular review of the scope of coverage of EA to ensure that these policy tensions are adequately balanced.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Part IV of the EA is important as it involves the "hours of work" and determines the scope of those who are entitled to overtime payments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The two current categories of workers entitled to overtime payments are, first, employees who are not a workman but who is covered under the EA and earns a monthly basic salary of not more than $2,500; and second, a workman earning a basic monthly salary of not more than $4,500.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Moving ahead, I also see a need to address whether the dichotomy between "workman" and "non-workman" is still tenable and whether it is also appropriate to consider extending the scope of Part IV to PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This may well be needed as the dichotomy between "Rank and File" and "PME" workers becomes increasingly blurred.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But it will require a closer and deeper examination as it will have a significant impact to both workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As shared earlier, PMEs earning above $4,500 are not protected by provisions in the EA, such as section 14 on wrongful/unfair dismissals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, the ECT does not have jurisdiction to hear wrongful/unfair dismissal cases under EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Currently, union members in unionised companies can file a case to the Manpower Minister for such unfair/wrongful dismissal cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, as we see more cases of workers, especially PMEs, facing such unfair/wrongful dismissals, it is also imperative that the Employment Claims Act be reviewed and the ECT’s jurisdiction be expanded to cover unfair/wrongful dismissal cases over and above the current salary-related claims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Another area for enhancement and greater clarity would be the very technical and highly moot provision of section 18A of EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In it, an employer has the right to transfer an employee to another employer if the organisation is being restructured.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I suggest we should consider amending section 18A to provide greater clarity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The other alternative would be to issue tripartite guidelines or an explicit articulation on what transfers or transactions fall within or outside of section 18A.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is one area that has constantly been tested and challenged, and greater clarity would be a boon for unions, employers and legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Many PMEs have approached us for help.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They face a lot of work-related problems, including unfair dismissal and also disputes related to EA.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, as some of these workers' monthly salary is more than $4,500, we are, therefore, unable to assist them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the past few years, the median income has been on the rise, and it applies to PMEs as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The proportion of PMEs in our workforce has also been increasing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To meet the needs of the future workforce and the requirements of jobs and workplaces in the future, I suggest we amend the EA in the following three areas.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We look forward to work with our unions/union leaders and our tripartite partners closely in the process of review and look forward to positive changes to the labour laws in this direction to better protect workers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that just under half of our resident employees would easily fall under the category of PMEs earning at least $4,500 a month.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, they are not protected under our EA.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is time that our EA be reviewed to ensure more of our workers are protected under it, particularly when retrenchments or employment disputes arise.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be good to increase the salary cap as there are more Singaporeans and resident employees who are now earning $4,500 a month and where we now also see more PMEs among Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Better still, remove the salary cap altogether so that all Singaporean employees, PMEs or otherwise, are protected under the EA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, the Tripartite Standard on Employment of Term Contract Employees was launched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a good first step in ensuring better protection of contract workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could the Minister give an update on how many contract workers are now covered under the Standard?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In her reply, Minister Teo said that the Standard relies on self-assessment by companies and engagements with employers based on complaints from employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand the Ministry's position to calibrate the compliance to give employers the incentive to adopt the Standard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there is also the need for the Ministry to do occasional audits to make sure that the Standard is meaningful for contract workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe many public agencies are hiring term contract workers and they should have adopted the Standard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, the Standard covers prorated leave benefits, adequate training and the notice period for early termination or non-renewal.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In November 2017, The Straits Times interviewed a 28-year-old female lawyer whose former boss repeatedly harassed her.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: After she rejected him again and again, her boss shifted her work away from legal work to menial tasks.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And though she reported her situation to all the appropriate levels of power, she was met with cultural roadblocks: a female senior colleague who told her to stay silent, a founding partner of the firm who brushed it off as "such things happen when you are a pretty girl", and a human resource (HR) department which advised her "not to make a fuss".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: After a year of feeling trapped, she confessed her story to her father – who was also a lawyer – who insisted that she make a Police report.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Scared for her future career prospects, she chose to inform the firm of her intentions to go to the Police.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The firm finally dealt with the matter by getting her to sign a non-disclosure agreement prohibiting her from reporting the matter to the Police.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In exchange, she received a year’s salary and had to leave the firm immediately.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The article said nothing further about the boss.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, for all we know, he is still out there harassing his employees.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The female lawyer told the reporter, "I am not someone who doesn't speak her mind.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But when I spoke up, I was told I'm a liar and I made things up.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that more people don't have to feel all alone and they can find some support." What is troubling about this story to me is that if a relatively well-resourced and legally trained employee with the support of a well-resourced and legally trained parent felt that helpless in the situation, how much more difficult would it be for an employee with less power and resources to seek help?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: First, the Tripartite Advisory to Manage Workplace Harassment is useful but there is no awareness about who is actually meeting those guidelines.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry consider having a public register that actually tracks which companies are adopting the measures suggested in the Advisory?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Second, because it is usually too complicated, expensive and ultimately pretty awkward to get a Court order against a colleague or boss, most victims do not bother with getting a protection order.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some victims also rather not immediately escalate their situation to the Police because they are uncertain about the impact on their personal safety and professional reputation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Harassment victims could benefit from having a safe and trusted third party with institutional authority to help them deal with their situation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) is an educational body and the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TDM) and ECT deal with more straightforward claims like salary disputes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: On FDWs, according to a March 2017 Singapore Law Review article, the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) "Employer’s Guide" is a good step.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But some of the language used in there is still a bit ambiguous.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Right now, words like "should" and "must" are used interchangeably in the guide.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But "should" is an aspirational goal whereas "must" sounds like an indisputable requirement.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, the guide uses "should" for "your foreign domestic worker should not sleep near any dangerous equipment or structure that could potentially cause hurt or harm to her, and "You and your foreign domestic worker should mutually agree on which day of the week she should take the rest day".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But it uses "must" for: "You must provide your worker with three meals a day" and "you must minimally provide your worker with a mattress, pillow and blanket".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This would help lessen public misunderstanding about what is MOM's tolerance level for abuse that an employer can get away with.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, on people with disabilities, the EA does not define what unfair dismissal is, leaving room for misunderstanding.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: People with disabilities have been dismissed without explanation by their employers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Since our workforce is rapidly ageing, acquired disabilities, such as mobility issues and sensory impairments, will become a growing challenge.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some employees also acquire a disability while working for a company.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, there is no requirement for a company to accommodate the employee’s changed situation, such as redesigning a job or offering an alternative role.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry require or assist employers to provide reasonable job accommodations for employees who acquire disabilities in the course of their employment so that they may continue in their current role, wherever this is possible or appropriate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: This is better than the economic growth in 2015 and 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: This was due to a larger drop in foreign employment, although local employment grew.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, it has been several years since Singapore started its economic transformation, focusing on productivity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share if this growth is sustainable and what can we do to maintain productivity growth?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, productivity growth is only meaningful in how they have benefited our workers who have dedicated themselves to helping companies to grow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How has the productivity growth resulted in better jobs and better wages for our workers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can we consider setting gains-sharing as a basic requirement for qualifying for Government funding schemes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Capital investment without complementary competent manpower impedes productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is important that our workers can take on new opportunities quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that MOM can also offer a Career Trial Programme to fresh graduates as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This helps them with finding an ideal job and lowers the attrition for the employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) has given mid-career Singaporeans a viable transition to another industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, many Singaporeans do not know about this good programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry consider working with organisations, such as the People’s Association (PA) and NTUC to promote and increase awareness of PCP?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am convinced that if the tripartite partners can work together, then the strong productivity growth last year will not be a one-off phenomenon.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Chairman, over the last two years' Committee of Supply (COS) debates, I have raised the issue about Singaporean and foreign workers, in terms of the Singaporean Core and the complementarity of local and foreign workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Can the Minister share on MOM's treatment of "Triple Weak" and "Triple Strong" companies?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I would also like to know if these efforts have resulted in better outcomes for Singaporeans, in particular, for our PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, in a May 2017 Business Times report, a headline read: "Tech talent shortage in Singapore unable to meet industry demands".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It quoted Hays Consultancy saying that employers were struggling to fill a number of tech roles, including cloud architects, cybersecurity professionals, data scientists and analysts, and mobile app developers.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In another report in August 2017, a Business Times’ headline read: "In the Asia Pacific, talent shortages will bite hardest in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How would the shortage impact Singapore’s overall competitiveness and ability to create jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How would MOM help employers, particularly those who are making efforts to raise productivity using technology, to recruit sufficient talents locally or overseas?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For new and special technical fields which our local institutions have not yet produced in the right numbers, would MOM allow firms to recruit more overseas talents in the interim?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, can the Minister provide an update on MOM's treatment of companies on the "Triple Weak" watchlist and of "Triple Strong" companies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have the "Triple Weak" companies been able to improve the Singapore Core in their workforce?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What improvements have been made in the HR practices of "Triple Weak" companies to build the strong Singapore Core?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have these resulted in Singaporean PMETs getting quality roles in organisations and seeing their incomes grow?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have we seen an increase of "Triple Strong" companies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the improving economic growth this year, are we seeing growth in PMET jobs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: More importantly, have Singaporean PMETs been able to qualify for these jobs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What more can be done to raise the number and quality of PMET jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am concerned if there continues to be missed match and mismatch of PMETs for the available jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have the various SkillsFuture programmes, like the Career Support Programme (CSP) and PCP, been able to address these gaps between jobs and the persons qualifying for these roles?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have businesses supported the PCP and CSP programmes?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What progress has been made for local PMETs on these programmes?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While there may be suitable job opportunities, are organisations with these PMET roles prepared to leverage these programmes to work with PMETs to transition into these roles?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we continue to focus on improving the quality of jobs for local PMETs, we must also recognise that with the pace of change and disruptions brought about by technological advancements, businesses do require new skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the short term, we may not have the skills and we are already hearing from businesses challenges in filling these roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This would mean that we will need to continue to tap on foreign talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Is there support available for businesses to strengthen the local-foreign manpower complementarity?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have been lobbying on strengthening the Singaporean Core, Fair and Progressive Hiring and eradication of nationality bias since 2011.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There are also greater focus and awareness of the move towards not just fair but progressive workplaces and employment practices by the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) and our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Anecdotally, the situation has improved when I speak to fellow PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: However, I do still hear complaints of two kinds.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: First, hiring-of-its-own-kind practices and companies advertising in the Jobs Bank for the sake of advertising and treating the FCF and the Jobs Bank as mere window dressing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This happens not just in big multinational corporations (MNCs) but also small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Some also share that employment agencies and placement companies are also where some of these malpractices happen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The general concern is over the glaring disproportionate number of foreign PMEs in certain sectors and companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In some cases, the nationality biasness results in job losses of local PMEs and hiring of foreign PMEs for jobs which local PMEs can fill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Has there been an improvement since the last time he shared about this "watchlist" and can he share what kinds of companies, whether MNCs or SMEs, and from what sectors these companies are from?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have five concrete suggestions for MOM in respect of what we can do.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can these areas be reviewed so that one is not easily exempted from the FCF requirements?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Suggestion 2 – Besides executive sanctions and measures, I suggest MOM can also recognise and offer "carrots" and recognition to those companies and businesses which demonstrate an exemplary Singaporean Core and a resolute commitment to hire and develop Singaporeans through the Human Capital Partnership programme (HCP).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Suggestion 4 – Over and above existing requirements under the law, there could be tighter regulation and accreditation of employment and placement agencies to weed out biased and unfair hiring-of-its-own-kind practices and ensure a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: By the same token, these agencies, recruitment companies and even company HR departments should not and must not treat the advertising requirement as mere window dressing, and their practices closely monitored.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Their frontline and placement staff should undergo mandatory training and accreditation to understand the concept of building the Singaporean Core, FCF and the Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want to remain highly attractive to companies around the world to draw their investments which will create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Investors and businesses, whether global or local, want access to global talent.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially so in high-tech companies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and robotics, where talents are in short supply and, hence, courted worldwide.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should welcome them because they bring unique value to the local economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we must ensure the transfer of expertise and technical know-how from these foreign employees to local employees within specific timeframes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such transfers are critical if we are to build a strong Singaporean Core and boost local competencies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How to facilitate these transfers is the challenge.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Monitoring and regulating the ratio and number of Singaporean staff at certain positions within companies after they have been occupied for a certain number of years by foreign staff is one way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Ministry have a process of tracking such data across industries?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another way is to require companies, in particular, those in critical sectors, to justify and limit the ratio of foreign hires and limit how long they can work here.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have to strike a balance between meeting their demand for selected foreign employees to work in Singapore and providing Singaporeans with job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: FCF seeks to ensure that Singaporeans are considered fairly for jobs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many employers are currently on the FCF Watchlist and which are the main sectors or industries where infringements occur?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Ministry also have the breakdown of the job categories, levels of seniority and salary ranges of jobs which had gone to the foreigners in these cases?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the main sources and channels of feedback, complaints and whistleblowing?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many Employment Pass (EP) applications by errant firms had been rejected by the Ministry in each of the last few years?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having such details will be useful for the Ministry to spot red flags, improve preventive measures and formulate better manpower policies to protect jobs for Singaporeans, as not all errant firms will be captured on the radar of FCF.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry also share with us the effectiveness of our National Jobs Bank in helping Singaporeans find jobs?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Ministry have some way of monitoring and evaluating the effectiveness and usefulness of this portal in ensuring that jobs are actually given to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, I would like to suggest that the Ministry consider doing so as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Should it be ineffective, we will have to come up with new strategies and ways to connect employers with Singaporean hires.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These are companies which have been identified as the Triple Weak companies and which do not adopt fair and progressive employment practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The companies employ foreign workers at the expense of Singaporean workers and this has created much unhappiness among Singaporeans who have lost their jobs or are employed by companies with a majority of foreigners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Their employment practice has also created much resentment among Singaporeans against foreigners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last month, during a house visit, my resident told me that her company has discriminatory practices in favour of foreigners because of the Managing Director's preference.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Despite my request, she did not wish to reveal the name of the company as she was concerned about her own employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: My concern is whether there are even more such Triple Weak companies which have discriminatory employment practices against Singaporeans and employ foreigners at the expense of Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can we consider revoking these companies' work passes or EPs of the foreigners in their companies?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We need to send a strong signal to such companies that if they are not interested in building a Singaporean Core and intend to hire mainly foreigners, then they should face the consequences as there is no purpose in allowing such companies to thrive in our business environment because they exist at the expense of the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can MOM consider enhancing this cap on a case-by-case basis based on sector-specific needs?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, I am glad to note that the SkillsFuture Leadership Development Initiative is steaming ahead and that more programmes are coming online under the initiative, such as the ASEAN Leadership Programme, to help Singaporean executives understand ASEAN business cultures better.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is important to ensure we cultivate a Singaporean Core in leadership positions across the economy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: CTP is another important initiative to be welcomed because it places Singaporeans at the heart of our economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: CTP will help to deepen knowledge transfers to Singaporean workers and train up a strong body of highly-skilled and continuous learning local workforce.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There must be concrete capability development, and this should be measurable.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I understand that CTP offers funding for industry-level projects, such as company-level projects.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: My concern with funding for company-level projects is that the capability transfer will be limited to benefiting a single company instead of the whole sector.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This means that the Government would end up supporting an uncompetitive situation in a sector.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For example, a large company dominating a sector could use CTP to acquire exclusive training for its staff, thereby enhancing its capability and competitive edge against other companies in the sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Thirdly, the median wages of semi-skilled workers have also gone up in the past years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I wish to ask if there are any safeguards to make sure that Singaporeans are not replaced by many of these younger, better educated S Pass holders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Is the scheme too attractive and flexible such that it will be abused?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, foreign workers form an integral part of Singapore's workforce.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In many sectors of the economy, foreign workers supplement the types of functions that local workers are not equipped to undertake and, thus, perform an indispensable role in our economic development.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the trend of the Government's manpower policy, businesses need to bring in foreign workers with a higher level of technical proficiency.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: While they are working, they also need to receive continual training, particularly in an environment characterised by rapid technological advances and industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As many enterprises are striving hard to transform, I hope the Government could support enterprises to manage these expenditures.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech at the Budget Debate, Mr Heng Chee How, Senior Minister of State cum NTUC's Deputy Secretary-General, emphasised that as our enterprises transform and upgrade, apart from the local workers, our foreign workers should also not be neglected.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the Government need not worry too much on how to support skills upgrading of foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This suggestion is based on the example of how the Government plans to use carbon tax in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the first five years of implementing the carbon tax, the Government plans to use the tax revenue to provide more grants and support to help enterprises enhance energy efficiency and reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the same way, instead of channelling foreign worker levies into other areas, I would suggest that the Government channel a portion of this levy towards training of foreign workers to uplift the overall skills level of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Further, the gig economy is rapidly emerging and has become a trend to be paid attention to.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Self-employed persons do not have regular employers, but this is precisely why many employers do regard them as a welcome addition to the workforce during the current manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is because companies always have certain projects which need to be managed by people with special expertise or talents.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If companies can find people with suitable criteria, and both parties agree to this flexible arrangement where the work is completed within a designated period, everyone would be perfectly happy.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Often this is also a more cost-effective solution.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Not long ago, in order to protect the rights of self-employed persons, the Government set up a Tripartite Workgroup (TWG) on Self-employed Persons to identify recommendations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister for Manpower has given his in-principle acceptance of these recommendations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We look forward to having these solutions rolled out as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Helping to alleviate the worries of these self-employed persons and building an even stronger and balanced employer-employee relationship is certainly good news to the business community all round!

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: To build a workforce with a strong Singaporean Core, we need Singaporean workers distributed across different sectors and at all levels of seniority and skills.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is important that we have our own local staff with technical competence and core skills for key sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: These shortages have resulted in dependency on foreign employees which, in turn, sometimes lead to communication difficulties due to cultural and language differences, or where even the hiring of foreigners is not enough to meet demand, we have to contend with long waiting times for repairs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is clear that hiring foreign employees in certain sectors is not a sustainable solution to labour shortage.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Minister share the details of the local workforce shortages in various sectors?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What measures do we have to boost the presence of local hires in these industries?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Companies must also restructure these jobs to meet the expectations of new local hires, in terms of pay, number of hours worked and job perception.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Companies should consider ways to differentiate themselves from their competition so that they can justify their higher fees and prices, in order to afford higher salaries to attract local employees.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In addition, companies can improve work conditions by tapping upon technological innovations to make such jobs either easier or safer, or both.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry share an update on the progress of this scheme?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, a key thrust of Budget 2018 is to drive pervasive innovation to support businesses to innovate across the entire value chain.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: LEDS, which was announced in 2015, is focused on helping businesses innovate and transform to become more manpower-lean and productive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, with digital disruption, business models are being challenged.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And to transform, businesses require a change of mindset and a re-imagination of their businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Have these companies been able to restructure jobs to become more attractive for workers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Given our ageing population, have the business transformation efforts made work processes more conducive for mature workers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I spoke in my Budget Debate speech on the benefits of businesses tapping on mature workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mature workers are a source of business experience but may have gaps in the new skills required for the jobs available.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: By making our workplaces more inclusive, businesses can benefit from the intergenerational diversity of their workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Given our tight labour market, especially for PMET roles, it would a shame for us not to tap the potential of this talent base.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Moving ahead, I hope to see even better use of the jobseeker, hirer, jobs and skills data in the Jobs Bank to help minimise both the missed matches and mismatches.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: As shared during my Budget Debate speech, I am particularly concerned about the three challenges of long-term unemployment, structural unemployment and underemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: It affects PMEs, mature PMEs, older PMEs and, increasingly, rank-and-file workers, too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I wish to ask MOM what has been done in the past three years to address the above challenges and how effective have the schemes been.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In particular, I have three suggestions for MOM to overcome some of these challenges.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: First, eradicate ageism and all hints of it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Till today, I still hear anecdotally of age discrimination amongst employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can we do more to get employers to be open in hiring and redesign their work and workplaces to cater to this group, instead of negating hiring them altogether?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second, expand support for employment facilitation and employment for both PMEs and rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The Labour Movement has carried out a detailed survey last year and the survey revealed that there are, indeed, mismatches of placement, skills and expectations, such as remuneration and job requirement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Of these, the mismatch of expectations between employer and worker is the most common occurrence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: By the same token, the type of mismatches differed between different sectors, such as the manufacturing sector and services sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: As the types of mismatches differ, the policy interventions must be customised to the needs of the sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In addition, the policies need to be dynamic to address the changing and evolving types of mismatches.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: It is, therefore, imperative to identify which form of mismatch a jobseeker is affected by and address it early lest it develops into another type of mismatch over time.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Chairman, Sir, last year, we experienced one of the best years in economic growth in recent memory.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: However, despite stronger than expected economic growth, long-term unemployment has been sticky.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The spike was mainly caused by older workers aged 50 and above and PMETs experiencing extended joblessness.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: In September 2017, according to MOM figures, the rate remained at 0.8%.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Older workers and PMETs again had lower rates of finding employment within six months than the overall rate.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Economists and the Government have explained the issue as caused by job-skills mismatches.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: New technologies and economic shifts have made many job functions and skills obsolete.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Therefore, it is good that the Government implemented programmes, such as the PCP and Place-and-Train (PnT) programmes in the last few years to help workers retrain and reskill.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Despite these programmes, long-term unemployment has remained sticky.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: PnT placed 1,800 workers, but only 5% were long-term unemployed workers.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Why are the programmes not helping enough long-term unemployed workers?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: What else can we do for the long-term unemployed workers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Many initiatives have been undertaken and enhanced, such as the enhanced PCP, the Attach-and-Train scheme, and the enhanced CSP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Will MOM similarly be doing more to help the rank-and-file workers?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With new schemes, such as CTP, it will be helpful to plug the gap in skillsets in certain important fields by supporting the transfer of skills from foreign specialists to fill the talent shortage, eventually to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Other Career Support Programmes (CSP), such as Work Trial and the new Career Trial Scheme, can be effective means for bold career switchers to not only switch industry, but also switch to different jobs to try them out before deciding to take on the job as a career.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should also identify the success rate of schemes like PCP and CSP in each and every ITM sector by focusing on it sector by sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For sectors where PCP or CSP is less popular or the dropout rate is high, we should address those concerns and put in place measures for these schemes to grow.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Conducting focus group discussions could be one way to better understand why certain schemes are less popular before we could tweak the programmes for better acceptance.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some other improvements could include mentors to provide support and longer work trial periods for better job assessment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, of the 223 Singaporeans from non-healthcare sectors who enrolled into the healthcare conversion programmes between 2009 and 2011, 82% completed their training and were successfully placed into a healthcare job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Among those successfully placed, 92% remained in their jobs after the end of the minimum service period.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can we define the minimum service period – the retention period – to be at least two years, so as to deem PCP as a successful placement?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For the 18% not successfully placed in the sector, what are the options for them?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What are the reasons for their unsuccessful placement?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For the 8% who left their jobs after their bonds, what are their reasons?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Were we able to keep them in the same industry?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Or had they left to return to their previous industry?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Would we be able to allow longer trial periods for individuals to ascertain their job fit for some of the professions?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, a psychometric test could be conducted for some of these professions to evaluate their suitability during the interview phase.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, this would provide a better return of investment for all parties that have put in efforts and resources to provide training opportunities and for those who had made the job switch.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, we could also examine the causal factor for dropout rates for the ITM sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The ultimate outcome is to develop skilled and productive workers for employers, a well-paying career for the individual, and, for the Government, one less unemployed worker to provide social support for.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I believe PCP and CSP are good steps to build a better skilled and productive workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Although this is not a large proportion of the workforce in numbers of persons, this is not insignificant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Digital platforms are making it more attractive for SEPs as they enable direct connections of those who provide services to those who need the services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This enables a sharing economy and potential efficiencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The profile of SEPs reflect the changes in our wider workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: A greater proportion are aged 50 and above.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There is also an increase in the share of those with tertiary education and they are also earning more, especially PMET SEPs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: On the part of businesses, digitalisation is also disrupting the way work is done, employment models and how businesses collaborate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Technological advancement is allowing greater flexibility of how and where work is done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Work can now be shared across different persons, and people do not need to be in the same time zones or same place to do work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We are already seeing this impacting many industries from healthcare, education, food and many other services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Businesses are not only directly employing their staff in regular employment but procuring relevant services of SEPs, as and when they are required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Hence, we will probably see an increasing trend of SEPs over time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can the Ministry share the responses to the TWG's recommendations to address these challenges?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, as mentioned by Ms Jessica Tan, freelancers or SEPs make up close to 10% of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The TWG was formed by the Minister for Manpower in 2017 to identify the main challenges faced and to make recommendations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have submitted our recommendations to the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to targeted assistance and specific support for our SEPs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In particular, I would like to draw our attention to a segment of SEPs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the Ministry’s assessment of this small but growing number?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, 17% did not engage in freelance work as a preferred choice.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Again, I would like to ask: what is the Ministry's assessment of this segment?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Did they fail in their efforts to seek permanent employment?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For working adults who are currently freelancers not as their preferred choice, what are the types of assistance available to help them transit to full-time employment?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For school leavers, are we able to strengthen our channels to guide our youths on the appropriate career choice to springboard their aspirations?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know we have Education and Career Guidance Counsellors (ECGCs) in schools, polytechnics or Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) and career coaches at the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) and Workforce Singapore (WSG) career centres to provide career guidance.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are these counsellors and coaches familiar with the nature of freelance work?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can they give a fair assessment of the risks involved, compared with permanent employment?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are they equipped with enough information, so as to better guide and advise their clients?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, I would encourage they enhance the support by collaborating with freelance groups to invite experts to mentor, conduct talks to share insights and raise greater awareness on the nature of freelance work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I worked as a freelancer for almost eight years between 2003 and 2011 in the Arts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Back then, my concern was whether I had enough jobs to ensure my financial survival in the short term.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At times, I would be offered part-time work with employer Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions, and that was a bonus and I felt more secure.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But by and large, the security of benefits, such as CPF provisions, was not something I thought much about.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: My experience then is similar to what freelancers face today, perhaps an exacerbated level in the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because of their relative lack of experience, they can be easily exploited by hirers offering them less pay.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure they get a job despite their lack of a portfolio, new entrants resort to undercutting, thereby creating a vicious cycle of decreasing wages.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They may take on more jobs than they can handle, endangering their own health and lives in some cases.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In full-time employment, there are legal and contractual obligations enshrining a social compact between employer and employee – employers' CPF contributions, paid sick leave, workplace insurance and other welfare.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But with a freelance engagement, the hirer does not bear such responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, sometimes, there is no agreement signed, no reimbursement for workplace injuries, no assurance of remuneration deadlines.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These are purely transactional relationships, where the hirer stands to gain because there is willing labour.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This freelance employment model will continue to thrive, because it is highly efficient.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is what the gig economy relies heavily on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As a first step, to ensure a fairer social compact, perhaps the Government can look at mandating hirers, probably starting from the Government agencies, to make contributions to CPF for the freelancers engaged.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The more they come together, the stronger their negotiating power.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It allows us to take care not only of ourselves, but of others like us.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It goes beyond the transactional because, through a social compact, we see our interdependency, thereby growing stronger as a society.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There is substantial evidence from public policy efforts that positive actions can be induced through non-compulsory incentive mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: SEPs typically face short-term cash flow needs, which may trump their longer-term economic interest in saving for future retirement.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: This was a slight dip from 60.4% for both 2016 and 2015.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: There are various reasons that women may choose not to work or be employed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: These reasons range from childcare or elderly care responsibilities to the decision to have a better work-life balance and work from home on a flexi-work basis.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: To what extent does our labour force participation rate data capture the proportion of women who are home-based entrepreneurs or who are on flexi-work schemes?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: What are some plans that the Ministry has to help and encourage more women to work or be economically active?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: To what extent have employers implemented flexi-work or work from home schemes to help our women who may wish to have a better work-life balance, and what more can we do, as a society and couples, better manage their familial and economic responsibilities more equitably, thus reducing the burden of familial responsibilities that rest on more women and reducing the burden of economic responsibilities that rest more on men?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: There are increasingly more women who are home-based entrepreneurs due to the work flexibility it provides.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How can the Government better support our home-based women entrepreneurs?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: What are some possible schemes or grants that can be made available to them, such as "micro-loans" or "seed" funding, for instance?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How else can the Government provide support for this network of home-based women entrepreneurs?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Another concern that I have is that women are still not seen as a valuable source of manpower in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Looking at the manpower statistics of 2017, more women are earning lower salaries compared to men.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I just cannot accept that women are less capable such that they deserve lower salaries or cannot be employed in positions that pay more for which they are given more responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I hope the Ministry will look into how employers employ the workers, particularly in ensuring that women are given equal opportunities, equal recognition and equal remuneration for jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mothers have experienced being treated harshly or assessed unfairly at work due to their pregnancy, and some have been dismissed subsequently upon their return from maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), it is unfair dismissal and maternity discrimination if an employer does not allow an employee to return to the same job after maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The International Labour Organization (ILO) Convention on Maternity Protection sets the international standard in guaranteeing a woman's right to return to the same position or an equivalent position paid at the same rate at the end of her maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: There are an increasing number of Singaporeans who have to take care of both younger children and older parents because of our marriage trends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: They will need greater support at the workplace to balance work-life responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The recent launch of the Tripartite Standard on Flexible Work Arrangements (TS-FWAs) is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: With the Tripartite Standard in place, there is an opportunity to accelerate adoption of FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: This would encourage employers to review existing structures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Our parents will also feel that they are less of an exception in working towards FWAs with their employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Understandably, companies, especially the smaller ones, might find it difficult to implement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The recent announcement on adjustment in work-life grant is particularly welcomed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Capabilities of the work-life consultants can also be enhanced to look into the process redesign and change management in companies which are really the key issues affecting FWA implementation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The other impact of balancing family needs is that our caregivers tend to drop out of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Our female residents, being the primary caregivers, have a lower workforce participation rate than their male counterparts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: They are also the primary caregivers, whether for children or their parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The consequence is less retirement savings due to the drop in CPF contributions during the years that they may have left the workforce to care for their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: How can the Ministry review the CPF cash and retirement sum top-up schemes to help our Singaporean women to be secure in their retirement?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: I urge the Ministry to adopt a more targeted approach in identifying the reason behind the low TS adoption rate.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: With the Government's role as a facilitator and enabler in the Industry Transformation Programme, can MOM tap on this engagement platform to better understand the concerns of companies?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: This also allows us to gather targeted feedback from the companies to improve the initiative.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: TS can help address two issues that may arise in any company in today's society – grievance handling and FWAs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Employers need to have established grievance handling procedures to ensure that employee issues are duly addressed and resolved.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: MOM can work with training providers to implement online resource platforms that allow management, HR and line managers to access the tools on handling employee grievances easily.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: MOM can also introduce examinable topics that line managers can take periodically to evaluate their standards as a TS adopter.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Another challenge is the need for FWAs in the workplace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Successful implementation of FWA can achieve win-win outcomes for both employer and employee.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: MOM and TAFEP can conduct regular dialogue sessions for companies and employees to share how they have benefited from adopting robust FWA practices.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: This will encourage more companies to adopt or review their existing FWA practice.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Currently, TAFEP focuses on incentivising companies to be TS adopters through positive publicity and added resources.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: These could include enterprise capability funds and employee support funds, such as WordPro, CSP and PCP and so on.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: This sends a clear message that the Ministry places strong emphasis on Fair Employment Practices.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: More should be done to raise public awareness on the TS so that our workforce recognises the TS adoption watermark as quality-assurance of that company.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in the last few months, the topic of sexual harassment in the workplace has been hotly discussed globally.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many, mostly women, have taken to social media to talk about their experience in facing and dealing with sexual harassment at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have also read press reports of such cases in the past year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there sexual harassment incidences happening at our workplaces which are not being surfaced?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Due to a variety of reasons, for example, out of fear of repercussions at the workplace, affected persons are highly and likely to be reluctant to report sexual harassment at their workplace, especially if the perpetrator is a superior.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially so if company policies are not explicit on what constitutes sexual harassment, and what standard of procedures are taken when reports are made.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Lim Swee Say had said that TAFEP works with NTUC and the Singapore National Employers' Federation (SNEF) to conduct regular courses to manage workplace harassment and have trained a fair amount of company representatives in the past two years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the measures in TAFEP guidelines are not prescriptive, and the Ministry does not track how many firms have implemented the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At present, the TAFEP guidelines are clear and good in giving specific guides to employers on what they can do to reduce incidences of workplace harassment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the guidelines still place a bit more emphasis on affected persons taking responsibility for their own workplace safety – keeping alert, looking out for signs, and understanding what constitutes harassment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is less emphasis, however, on educating staff on how to not harass, and the consequences of doing so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The guidelines also do not illuminate on sexual harassment in detail.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As seen in recent debates around the globe, it can be sometimes ambiguous to perpetrators on what constitutes sexual harassment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such guidelines can include clearer definitions of sexual harassment as well as to take into account the concerns I have raised earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM should also keep track of companies which have implemented the recommendations made in the guidelines, and whether guidelines are followed through in reported cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may provide a better picture so as to help the Ministry as well as non-government organisations (NGOs) to take a more focused approach to handling all related issues more effectively.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does the Ministry have the gender breakdown for this group that meets the Basic Retirement Sum?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Are women as equally represented in this group as men?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Is more being done to encourage top-ups and transfers?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This means that we have a substantial number, most of whom are low-income earners, who will barely have enough for retirement.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We have not even included the numbers of those who are not active CPF members.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does the Minister also have the projections for the amount needed each month for an individual in retirement in the next 10, 20 and 30 years?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Based on these projections, the Basic Retirement Sum drawdown forms what proportion of the total amount needed?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is a global phenomenon that life expectancy is increasing in many countries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Studies show that global life expectancy will increase, on average, by two and a half years every decade, or an increase of three months every year or six hours every day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore's life expectancy is increasing by three and a half years every decade.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, if you were born between the 1960s and 1980s like me, half of us can expect to live for over 90 years.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For those born from 2000 onwards, 50% can live beyond 100 years.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I had made a call in my Budget speech for our tripartite partners to consider gradually making employers’ CPF contribution rates to be the same for all workers up to 67 years of age to help with retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I do acknowledge it will be difficult for the tripartite partners to reach a common consensus.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the circumstances, perhaps MOM can help members to get better returns from the CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS).

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Minister mentioned last year at COS that MOM will review the CPFIS to better serve the interest of CPF members.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am concerned that some members are investing through the CPFIS even though they are not financially knowledgeable.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They may not fully understand the risks and costs involved, and this could be detrimental to their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on this review, in particular, with regard to how we can help CPF members have better awareness on how much they actually understand the financial implications before they decide whether to invest their CPF savings?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Chairman, Sir, I have argued in my Budget Debate speech that Silver Support payouts to needy seniors based on HDB flat type may cause hardship for the seniors as well as send the wrong signals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Seniors who meet the criteria for Silver Support are already means-tested to be requiring cash support to meet their everyday needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: They are rigorously means-tested to have low lifetime wages, live in an HDB flat, not own large properties and have low household support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The seniors who qualify for Silver Support are already means-tested to be needy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The size of the flat that they happen to live in does not make them more or less needy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Many seniors often do not have a choice of which son or daughter to live with, or the size of the flat could be a legacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Having payouts tiered according to flat types seems to signal two things to seniors and their families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: One, it is better for a senior to stay with the child with a smaller flat or to live alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Two, it is better for the family to downgrade to a smaller flat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: These signals go against the thrust to get our seniors to age in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I also have several questions to address other specific concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The Minister had said that seniors who did not qualify for Silver Support could appeal for a review of eligibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: How many appeals have been received so far?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What were the main reasons when the appeals were not approved?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: On the appeal process, how can a senior make the appeal?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What documents or documentation are required for the appeals?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, when we discuss retirement adequacy, we speak of replacement rates – the ratio of retirement income to pre-retirement earnings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nowadays, many PMETs are finding themselves retrenched, being unemployed for stretches of time, and/or having to take pay cuts later in life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, the replacement rate from just CPF LIFE payouts may increase as a result of their income dropping later in life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the case of people who are in this at-risk group who have already reached a CPF Minimum Sum, and who can show their income has dropped severely, can MOM consider allowing them on an appeal and for a limited time to contribute a smaller amount in employee CPF so as to free up more cash for their day-to-day needs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That would mean that their CPF does not grow quickly and would get less CPF LIFE payouts when they retire, but they will still get their CPF LIFE payout generated by the Minimum Sum.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if their working income has dropped drastically, then their smaller CPF LIFE payout in future would still achieve a reasonable replacement rate with less employee CPF paid for some years prior to retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This gap stands at 18% and has not changed in a decade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It suggests we have hit a structural limit to closing the gap by improving the educational attainment of women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: To put it simply, this structural limit is that women's participation in the workforce tends to follow the M-curve, leaving employment in their 30s and 40s to provide caregiving for children or aged parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In general terms, the current gender income gap means that women will have 18% less CPF savings than men when they enroll in CPF LIFE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: With the gender differentiated premiums, women will get less income per month from CPF LIFE than men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The argument for gender differentiated CPF LIFE payouts is that it is fair because women as a group live longer than men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The corollary is that a unisex CPF LIFE with the same payouts for men and women will make men "cross-subsidise" women for living longer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I do not know why men "cross-subsidising" women so that everyone can have a reasonable retirement income until they pass on is so terrible a notion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Let us take a step back and consider this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Women are already disadvantaged by the gender income gap and the unpaid caregiving in the middle of the M-curve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Should not women be given the slight advantage at the end of their lives, just in terms of CPF LIFE payouts, for the sacrifices they willingly take up during the most productive phase of their lives?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The other argument for gender differentiated CPF LIFE payouts is that it is following the industry norm for annuities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But CPF LIFE is not a commercial product sold by a private insurer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is a national pension programme that combines commercial standards and the social protection concerns of a progressive Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The retirement inadequacy of women is a major social protection concern in our ageing society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: More than half of these older family caregivers do the work alone.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In another Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) survey on informal caregiving, it was shown that caregivers experienced substantial stress due to financial stress arising from caregiving.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: This was especially acute with younger caregivers because of their multiple commitments, as these so-called "sandwich" caregivers have to work, tend to their children and care for their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: If we aspire to be a caring society, then we cannot be negligent towards caregivers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: The elderly folks taking care of their spouses, caregivers for the disabled, or the above mentioned "sandwich" caregivers, they deserve our support and utmost respect.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In Australia, allowances are given to those with heavy and regular caring duties that result in forgone earnings.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In Norway, municipalities which are responsible for long-term care services employed family caregivers directly and provide a wage and insurance plan.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We could also introduce a long-term care (LTC) insurance plan, and LTC insurance which individuals can tap on to pay for their own LTC arrangements as well as those of their family members.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: This would be similar to funds in Germany where social security or LTC insurance can be used for oneself or one's family members.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: With our greying population, the burden of caregiving will increase significantly.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: To be a truly compassionate society, we need to put in place structures of support for the caregivers in our midst.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: It has been reported that while our unemployment level remains low, there are substantial numbers of jobseekers who have been out of work for at least six months and who have found it difficult to get new employment.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: In other words, they are considered to be facing long-term unemployment.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How effective have the PCP, CSP or Adapt and Grow (A&G) schemes been in helping older workers aged 50 and above to re-enter the job market?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How many of our older workers have managed to draw a salary equivalent to their last drawn salary after undergoing PCP, CSP or A&G as they re-enter the job market?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
