text: How many have managed to see an increase in their monthly salary after having gone through PCP, CSP or A&G?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: I would also like to urge the Ministry to consider reviewing the CPF contribution rates for older workers aged above 55.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: As we encourage Singaporeans to continue to stay active, be gainfully employed and financially independent and make their golden years count, the Government also needs to help them to do so.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: At the age of 55 or 56, many Singaporeans are still supporting school-going children as well as elderly parents and are still paying for their housing loans.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Drastically reducing the monthly CPF contributions by 11% when they reach 56 years old would mean that they would need to pay more of their housing loan in cash or that they would need to pay for their children's post-secondary tuition fees in cash.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Bearing in mind that more Singaporeans are marrying later and having children later, this situation will be experienced by more Singaporeans as we live through this decade and the next couple of decades.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Many Singaporeans still want to work and be gainfully employed between the ages of 56 and 60, as they still have financial commitments to fulfil.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Between the age of 56 and 60, many Singaporeans are still healthy and active, both physically and mentally, and are still able to actively and productively contribute to their work and fulfil their job responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: If retaining the CPF contribution rates for this group of Singaporeans would render them less attractive to be employed, there are two suggestions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: One, the CPF contribution rates can be staggered downwards progressively rather than a drastic cut once they cross the threshold of 55 to 56 years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For instance, upon reaching 56, the employer CPF contribution can be 16% and the employee CPF contribution can be 19%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Upon reaching 57, their employer CPF contribution can be 15% and the employee contribution can be 18%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The reduction goes down progressively 1% to 2% a year until they reach 60.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Two, the Government can come in to provide a buffer for CPF reduction in a bid to encourage older Singaporeans to continue to work, be financially independent and stay active.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Where employers are reluctant to continue to pay the more than 13% CPF contribution, the Government can step in and plug the gap.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For instance, upon reaching 56, the employer contributes CPF at the rate of 13% while the Government contributes 3%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: They have a wealth of historical and institutional knowledge as well as work-related experiences that can be tapped on.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Employers should find ways in which older workers, if they are less physically able to continue to perform the work that they have been doing, can undergo job redesign to become trainers or mentors to younger workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: It is a waste of talent and experience to let older Singaporean workers retire or even end up doing menial work.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, we can expect older workers to comprise an increasing proportion of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Some seniors will even continue working beyond the re-employment age of 67.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We should support those who wish to remain active at work to contribute their experience and expertise.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Job redesigning and the implementation of age-friendly work practices will become increasingly important and pervasive across different industries and sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What is the sectoral breakdown for the companies which had applied successfully?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does the Ministry have information on the penetration rate for different sectors and why some sectors attract more successful applications than others?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I would also like to ask about the proportion of companies which enjoyed productivity gains after job redesigning with the grant.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Since so many firms have utilised the grant, is there a platform for best practices to be shared so that other companies can benefit from faster and smoother workplace or workflow redesign to better suit older employees?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What measures does the Ministry have to raise awareness about the availability of the grant and share the stories of successful applications?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Could the Ministry make it mandatory for all public contracts for tender to include a term and condition that suppliers have to adopt these age-friendly practices?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Due to the emergence of new technologies, all of us must be prepared to do things differently for the same jobs or experience career conversions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Such changes are challenging for many senior workers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does the Ministry have details of the number of beneficiaries in various age groups?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What is the proportion of individuals aged 60 and above?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does the Ministry have plans to allocate more resources to train and support seniors who make such career transitions?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry also share a progress report about older lower- to middle-income workers involved in the Work Trial scheme which enables them to try out new careers?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What is the success rate and how many workers above the age of 60 have benefited?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sadly, they could only turn to menial jobs that are physically demanding.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead as our economy evolves, there will be fewer jobs that demand labour but more jobs requiring intellectual wisdom.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The elderly tomorrow will be better-educated and tech-savvy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we do not combat ageism now and start changing how we structure work, everyone will soon lose out, especially as our population ages rapidly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To be clear, this is not to ask for special privileges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But what if a senior candidate is denied the chance, not because of his innate ability, but because the work environment, process and job roles were designed against them?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, it is imperative to create employment opportunities for seniors and a favourable environment to help them thrive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is MOM doing to stamp out ageism?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Would MOM consider adding teeth to the legislation?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Alas, legislation is a crude though effective way of combating ageism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More importantly is how do we redesign the workplace and work for seniors?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Apart from the grants available, could the Government take the lead in testing how work environment, workflows, job role designs and compensation and benefits, such as health benefits, CPF contributions and leave conversion, can be adapted and optimised for senior workers?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some may choose to volunteer or pursue unfulfilled dreams.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But let us just make the workplace elderly-friendly and give the seniors an option to decide for themselves.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Perhaps, resources could be pooled by companies in the industry to develop best practices, to modify tools and equipment for use off-the-shelf by older workers throughout the industry?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: As businesses in our industries think about how to change, even disrupt, processes in the workplace in order to generate greater value on the back of better-used resources, could we make Job Redesign for Older Workers a required part of the syllabus?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: We know productivity is one of the four pillars supporting the growth and competitiveness plans of an ITM.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Could we envision Job Redesign for Older Workers as a key component of ITMs: a third Horizontal, along with promoting ICT adoption and Skills development?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: It can help to support the industries and produce improvements across the economy in the face of an ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Despite the publication of fair employment practices by MOM, accounts of employment discrimination remain.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The same survey also said that 20% of the Malay respondents and 18% of the Indian respondents and respondents of other ethnicities said that they very often or always felt discriminated against when applying for work.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such responses suggest that the current Fair Employment Practices under TAFEP have not addressed discriminatory employment practices as successfully as it could, even if the number of such complaints has, indeed, gone down over the past year.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If anything, these surveys show a possible under-reporting of discriminatory employment practices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The issue with discrimination and discriminatory practices is that people can feel and believe that they are not behaving in a discriminatory fashion when they actually may be.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask how the Ministry would work and also to better communicate with various stakeholders to fulfil the Government's commitments under the Convention to better deal with discrimination.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Would MOM consider working with the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) to strengthen existing enforcement procedures against discriminatory employment practices?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Chairman, Sir, in many jurisdictions, there are laws that ban the use of pre-employment questionnaires asking jobseekers about their mental health, to reduce discrimination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In 2016, the Minister replied to my question on doing the same here that such declarations will not disqualify a candidate from being considered for the job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In October 2016, The Straits Times reported on employment discrimination faced by people with mental illness, in which several interviewees said that they felt the “sense of societal rejection most acutely while job hunting".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I understand that job applicants who think they have been discriminated against could report the case to MOM, which will then investigate to make sure that the employers are conducting fair and progressive recruitment practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The problem is that hard evidence of discrimination often does not exist, as the discrimination is often not communicated or is only verbally communicated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The culture of inclusive and progressive employment is setting in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The mindsets of employers and consumers have been changing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I believe the Government could and should extend the same experience to promote the inclusive employment of people with mental illness and change the prevailing prejudices against mental illness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The World Health Organization has estimated that, in developed economies, one in four people have a mental illness some time in their lifetime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Inclusive employment of people will go a long way towards combating society’s prejudices against mental illness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Inclusive employment will assure people with mental illness that seeking help for their illness will not prevent them from gainful employment in the future which, in turn, will help them integrate into society and minimise relapses.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Zainal Sapari, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: The effects of the PWMs are not one-off.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: It also helps the service providers to manage business cost better when they bid for contracts as the future manpower cost is more predictable.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Would MOM look at extending the PWM to more sectors, such as through industry-led or voluntary arrangements?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I would also like to ask what more can be done to improve their wages and employment conditions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Could we review the EA to make it more pro-low-wage workers?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: For example, could the pay for working on the rest day be standardised, regardless of whether it is at the request of the employee or employer?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Many employers now find ways to pay only the lower rates applicable for work done at employees’ request although it is really them who made the request.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Could the Annual Wage Supplement (AWS) be made mandatory?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Could we explore the possibility for employers to pay the medication cost for outpatient treatment done at company-appointed clinics or Government polyclinics for non-chronic illnesses?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: In the low-wage sectors, such as construction, landscape and security, the workers often find themselves deployed at various sites throughout Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: At these places, companies may provide good, proper rest areas for their permanent employees.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: However, when it comes to the outsourced workers who slog at these sites, they often find that there are no proper rest areas provided to them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Neither are they allowed to share rest areas provided to the permanent employees.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: These workers also put in effort and hard work into their job duties, and the fruits of their labour often result in a better environment for everyone at the site.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, in our national quest for industry transformation, many sectors are focused on technology adoption, productivity improvement and workforce development.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are important, but it is critical that we do not take WSH for granted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the contrary, we must constantly ask ourselves how can we make WSH more pervasive in every workplace?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Finland, it is mandated that there must be one elected Occupational Safety and Health representative in workplaces where there are at least 10 employees working regularly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Should Singapore have a mandatory WSH officer in every company?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For now, companies must appoint a Risk Management Champion (RMC) for BizSAFE Level 2.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With structured training, we believe that the role of these RMCs can be expanded to serve as WSH representatives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With more WSH-trained staff on the ground, one area that we can do better moving forward is to encourage better near-miss reporting to reduce the occurrence of accidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A structured and well-participated near-miss reporting regime would help to better identify dangerous work conditions and early interventions can help bring down the accident rate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While it is important to have preventive measures to reduce workplace injuries, it is equally important to help workers return to work in the unfortunate event of an accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MOM provide an update on employers’ participation in near-miss reporting and the RTW Programme?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans to make participation in these two initiatives mandatory in the years ahead?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, the RTW grant is currently restricted to SMEs and does not cover cases involving vocational rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To promote and deepen the RTW culture, can MOM consider extending the grant to non-SMEs as well as to cover vocational rehabilitation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While much of our WSH efforts today focus on workplace safety, physical health and mental well-being seem to have been neglected in our WSH efforts and conversations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With an ageing workforce, workplace health issues will likely become more prevalent in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Prolonged exposure to health hazards at work may result in work-related illnesses, some of which may even be irreversible.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A build-up of stress and fatigue can also lead to distractions, raising the risk of getting injured at work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Occupational health management is, therefore, critical to ensure that our workers are healthy at work and can perform their roles effectively and productively.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Beyond workplace safety, are there any upcoming plans by MOM on workplace health issues as part of Total WSH?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as we have Total Defence, we must endeavour to have Total WSH.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Workplaces are generally regarded as safe physical environments by most.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: However, it is increasingly common for employees to be subjected to abuse or harassment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: It can be physical, verbal and even via the Internet.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Hence, there is a greater need for awareness and protection against all workplace abuse and harassment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: I advocate strongly for all organisations to adopt zero tolerance towards abuse and take firm steps to stamp out errant behaviours.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: All employees must be informed on the reporting and response procedure for workplace abuse and harassment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Workplace harassment includes any conduct or behaviour that violates another person's dignity or create an unfavourable work environment, thereby posing a risk to that person’s safety and health.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: More can be done to educate employees on how to respond to workplace abuse and harassment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Often, the psychological trauma is neglected, but the long-term effect to overall wellness is no less severe.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: It is important to understand the scale of the problem.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Collating relevant statistics would allow for an in-depth study to identify possible interventions effectively.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: This will help to reduce the administrative and financial burden through Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: It is, indeed, alarming that in recent months, there have been several incidents of online criticism of Public Service sector staff.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: I am very concerned about the growing trend of such a campaign as it will inevitably lead to cyber-flaming.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Without the benefits of complete information, it is nearly impossible to determine the validity of the claim of either party.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Affected employees will be subjected to greater distress and psychological trauma as a result, while the perpetrator gets away scot-free.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: This would also involve public education and, more importantly, how to provide the relevant psychological support for affected staff at the workplace.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, could you take your two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Yet, these are merely the cases that have come to light.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Therefore, even in cases when these workers are underpaid or not paid, or when they experience safety violations, they would rather stay silent, to avoid losing their jobs and, by extension, their ability to repay their debts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: To target the root cause of these problems, I would like to ask the Ministry to look into helping these workers to reduce their recruitment costs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In last year's COS, I have spoken about recruitment approaches in Korea, in which the Ministry has said that they would look into.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I would, therefore, like to ask for an update on this issue.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: At the same time, the Jobs Bank provides an added benefit of transparency.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Jobseekers from Singapore or overseas can access the same vacancies directly without any interference from middlemen or recruitment agencies.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Could we, therefore, look into extending this approach to other foreign non-domestic Work Permit vacancies?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: This infrastructure that we already possess with the Jobs Bank can be applied here as a viable ready-made solution.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: By reducing the burden of recruitment costs, foreign workers will have improved mental health states, thereby increasing their productivity and overall work safety levels.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Also, they will not shy away from reporting errant employers who flout workplace safety regulations or unjustly withholding pay.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: The second issue of concern I would like to bring up is the non-issuance of contracts to foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Yet, upon arriving in Singapore, many either realise that they have been duped by forged IPAs or that their key employment terms (KET) issued within 14 days of starting work, are not aligned with the IPAs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In fact, this KET does not even need to be signed nor is it an actual employment contract.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: MOM's newly-announced Settling-in Programme for male construction workers could be an opportune time to educate the workers about KETs and employment contracts as well.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We must ensure that our workers are accorded rights and protection against abuse.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We should, therefore, do our best to ensure that our foreign workers, often tasked with hard, menial labour to build our roads and homes, are working under humane conditions and never exploited.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, one-third of our current workforce are migrant workers, and it is imperative that we continue to look into their well-being and ensure that they are fairly treated while working here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Through the work of NTUC's Migrant Workers Centre, we have identified salary-related disputes as one of the most common issues affecting migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: To minimise such disputes, how is MOM encouraging our employers to use electronic payment for their migrant workers' salaries?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Migrant workers here often worry about losing their jobs should they raise a complaint with the authorities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: To encourage early reporting of salary-related cases, can MOM consider doing some degree of matching between companies submitting new Work Permit applications for fresh workers and migrant workers here who have requested for a change of employers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Today, there are various efforts by different organisations to orientate new migrant workers who arrive in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Does MOM have any plans to synergise these various efforts to holistically orientate and integrate our migrant workers, particularly in their early days in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: A one-stop help centre can also serve to be a valuable resource and avenue of support throughout their stay here while working.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Many companies today still focus on quantity, instead of quality, when looking to hire migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Where possible, employers should leverage the experience of their current migrant workforce and do more to upskill them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In line with Singapore's overall productivity effort, will MOM introduce new measures to encourage employers to bring in higher-skilled migrant workers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Does MOM have any plans in 2018 to further tighten the in-flow of migrant workers in terms of skills and competencies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As we move into a cashless society, there is no doubt that all migrant workers will have a bank account.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In addition, their laws require banks, payroll outsourced providers or employers themselves to certify monthly that full salaries have been paid, creating an early-warning system for the authorities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission, I have asked the Clerk to place the MOM COS-in-brief on the seats of the Members at the start of the Sitting.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Mr Chairman, may I also seek your permission to display some slides on the LED screen?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The employment landscape has changed in the past three years from 2015 to 2017, compared to the previous three years from 2012 to 2014.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The long-term unemployment rate went up, too, to 0.8% in September 2016.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The reasons were partly cyclical but mostly structural: externally, faster pace of technology and innovation and keener and stronger competition; internally, ageing of the local population and the changing profile of our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Manpower-driven growth of the past was no longer sustainable.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Low productivity growth will weaken our economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Fast growth of foreign manpower will increase social tension and weaken our social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is why we have to transform our economy to be more innovative, manpower-lean and productive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we transform, we are mindful that one main concern out there is about jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Will we end up with "jobless growth" for our people?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Lee Yi Shyan, Mr Desmond Choo and Asooc Prof Faishal Ibrahim asked whether our locals have benefited from the economic growth and transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Again, comparing the past three years from 2015 to 2017 with the previous three years from 2012 to 2014, even though growth of foreign employment has turned negative, local employment growth has rebounded to 21,000 last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: PMET share of the local workforce went up faster in the past three years than the previous three years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In terms of wage growth, annualised real income growth of our residents for the previous three years is shown in grey and, for the past three years, it is shown in pink.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, grey means 2012 to 2014, and pink means 2015 to 2017.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We can see that real income grew faster across all income groups, up from 2.3% to 3.7%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We can also see that wages at the 20th and 30th percentiles (P20 and P30) not only grew faster than before but also higher than most income groups.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are certainly in a better shape today.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having transformed from a high manpower growth, low productivity gain of 4 + 0.4 = 4.4, or 4% manpower growth and 0.4% productivity growth, to give us 4.4% gross domestic product (GDP) growth, from 2012-2014, we have transformed to 1 + 1.8 = 2.8 in the last three years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is, 1% manpower growth and 1.8% growth in productivity, to give us the average of 2.8% growth on GDP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are now much closer to our future growth strategy of 1 + 2 = 3.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if the productivity growth is sustainable.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To make transformation and productivity growth more sustainable, we must press on with four key thrusts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And these are: better job growth in our economy; better employment outcomes for our people; better protection for our workers; and lastly, better capabilities in our Singapore Workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must also keep improving the quality and attractiveness of jobs to meet the higher aspirations of our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, instead of developing Lean Enterprises individually, we need to develop Lean Industry collectively, especially for sectors that are less attractive to locals today.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Even though the resident unemployment rate has declined since June last year, we are still concerned that unemployment in future is likely to be stickier, not due to shortage of jobs but shortage of skills and job-skill mismatches.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I think the concern was also shared by Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have enhanced the national Jobs Bank into an online job portal known as MyCareersFuture.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are also strengthening the Adapt and Grow Initiative to minimise missed matches and mismatches.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For our older workers, the re-employment age was raised from 65 to 67 last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Employment rates for mature workers aged 55 to 64 and 65 and over, have continued to improve.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are also actively promoting more companies to make better use of technology to make jobs Easier Safer and Smarter (ESS) for our mature workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Dr Intan Mokhtar suggested raising their CPF contribution rates.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Heng Chee How suggested to review the need for statutory retirement and to raise re-employment age further beyond 67.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The issues raised by Mr Heng, Mr Zainal Sapari and Dr Intan are important issues.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We introduced the PWM for cleaning in 2014, followed by landscaping and security two years later in 2016.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A few days ago, I came across a Straits Times article by NUS economists Kenneth Ler and Ivan Png titled "Impact of Progressive Wage Model", and I quote, "In sum, as a unique kind of "minimum wage" policy, the PWM has succeeded in raising wages without apparently reducing employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: More importantly, as a tailored, structured and progressive policy, it provides a wage ladder for low-skilled Singaporean workers, holding out its promise of growing income over time." Sir, we will make the adoption of PWM more widespread to benefit more workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Minister of State Sam Tan will elaborate later.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the growth of the platform economy, we can expect to see more freelancers and SEPs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are concerned for them in terms of skills upgrading, fair treatment, loss of income due to injury or illness and savings for healthcare and retirement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Minister Josephine Teo will elaborate on this later.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the vast majority who still engage in jobs with the employer-employee relationship, Mr Patrick Tay and Dr Intan Mokhtar called for a review of the EA.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, all workmen who are manual workers or blue-collar workers, including most technicians; second, all non-workmen who are non-manual workers or white-collar workers; and lastly, some but not all managers and executives with a salary cap of $4,500.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With PMETs making up 56% of the local workforce now, going up to 65% by around 2030, it is timely to make a more fundamental change to the coverage of EA.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In consultation with the tripartite partners, we have decided to enhance our current EA framework.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I am sure Mr Patrick Tay must be very happy to hear this because he has been championing this for many years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The exceptions are public servants, domestic workers and seafarers who are covered separately, such as by other Acts due to their nature of work.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for more clarity on the types of transfers within or outside the scope of section 18A about sale of businesses and business restructuring.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will work with the tripartite partners to update our guidelines on this.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Second, we will extend additional protection on hours of work and overtime payment to more workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As for overtime pay, the salary cap for non-workmen will be revised upwards, from $2,250 to $2,600.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: About 100,000 non-workmen will benefit from this increase.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The third and final change to the EA concerns dispute resolution relating to salary disputes or wrongful dismissal.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Currently, all salary-related disputes are mediated at TADM.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If unresolved, the claims are heard at ECT.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But wrongful dismissals are adjudicated by MOM, not ECT.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh spoke about protection for contract workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The tripartite partners launched the Tripartite Standard on the employment of term contract workers in July last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For contracts of 14 days or more, the Standard calls for companies to treat contracts renewed within one month from end of previous contract as continuous and cumulative in terms of length of service, for the computation of leave benefits and the notice period for early termination or non-renewal.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It also calls for companies to provide training to ensure that their contract workers can perform their roles effectively.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked for an update.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As of end February, more than 550 employers, covering more than 30,000 term-contract employees, have adopted this Standard.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So far, we have not received any complaint from any of these contract employers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh also suggested that we should conduct audits and surveys, and to include retrenchment benefits in the Standard.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Being a new Standard, the focus now of the tripartite partners is to increase the adoption by more employers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we will look into the suggestions by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh when we next review the Standard.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Through joint efforts of the tripartite partners, our WSH performance has improved.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The fatality rate has dropped to 1.2 last year, the lowest level ever recorded for our workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our next target, under WSH 2028 to be formulated, is to bring it down further to below one per 100,000 workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are also committed to reduce workplace injuries as well as to enhance workplace health by embracing a mindset of Total WSH.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Minister of State Sam Tan will elaborate later.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last but not least, our fourth and probably one of the most critical challenges is to ensure that slower growth of our Singapore Workforce will not become the bottleneck in the future growth of our Singapore Economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, our Singapore Workforce of 3.4 million is made up of 2.3 million locals, two-thirds of the total workforce; and 1.1 million foreigners, one-third of our total workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, "two-thirds" local plus "one-third" foreign give us "one" Singapore Workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With slower manpower growth into the future, we need to maximise the potential of our two-thirds local and our one-third foreign so that, together, we can maximise the potential of our Total Singapore Workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must strive for two-thirds plus one-third is not just equal to one, but greater than one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, we must not allow two-thirds plus one-third to be less than one, and this could happen if unfair employers discriminate against our local workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To prevent this from happening, we are pro-business but only to those businesses which are pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They have the preconceived ideas that our local PMETs are either unable or unwilling to do the job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, they write them off without even considering them fairly.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We, therefore, put them on our FCF Watchlist.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Their EP applications are subjected to additional scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is to eradicate "nationality bias", as described by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In response to Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Chong Kee Hiong, these companies on our Watchlist come from various sectors, including employment agencies and placement companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim asked for an update.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: TAFEP worked with them to improve their HR practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: WSG, NTUC-e2i and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) worked with them to recruit fresh graduates and our mid-career local PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One of these companies is an IT services firm with more than 1,000 PMET employees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It was placed on the Watchlist in February 2016.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The company worked with TAFEP and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) to attract and retain locals and hired about 200 more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: After exiting from the Watchlist, this company continues to adopt fairer and more progressive HR practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Indeed, these are win-win outcomes for both the business and the workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Another example, a private wealth management company with 80 PMET employees used to hire mostly foreign PMETs to serve mostly expatriate clients.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It was placed on the Watchlist in February 2016.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Since then, it has repositioned to serve both local and expatriate clients, and they hired 30 Singaporean wealth managers and PMETs, trained them here as well as overseas.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Second, for "two-thirds plus one-third, greater than one", we will make the "two-thirds local" better and strengthen our local core.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I agree with Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Lim Biow Chuan.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will continue to enhance the employment and employability of Singaporean PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will create more jobs of the future for them through Industry Transformation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will create more skills of the future in them through the SkillsFuture movement, and we will create more careers of the future with them through the Adapt and Grow initiative.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, it will also cover more jobs with a salary of up to $12,000 as of today, to jobs with a salary of up to $15,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This will take effect from 1 July this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we moderate the intake of foreign manpower, especially foreign professionals, employers say they cannot find enough locals who have the skills and are willing to do the jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They say this has slowed down their pace of business transformation and growth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They feel our foreign manpower policy is too tight.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But on the other hand, we hear ground feedback that there are still too many foreigners, too much competition here for jobs with our locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They feel that our foreign manpower policy is too loose.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, to them, MOM is not pro-worker enough.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We, therefore, stay open to the intake of foreign professionals, but continue to tighten the criteria for EP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is to calibrate the growth of EP holders and enhance their overall quality, both at the same time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim asks for the outcomes.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the past three years, on average, we approved about 50,000 new EPs every year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But at the same time, about the same number of EPs were not renewed, and the growth of EPs, therefore, slowed to an average of 3,000 a year in the past three years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is significantly lower than the peak of 32,000 in one year, in 2011.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the whole, the local share of net growth in PMET employment improved from an average of 68% in the previous three years – 2012 to 2014 – to an average of 78%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, from 68%, it went up to 78% in the past three years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Out of every 10 net increase in PMET jobs in the last three years, seven to eight of them went to our local PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Sectors where locals accounted for a large majority of the net growth in PMET employment include professional services, infocomm, healthcare, finance and insurance.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In short, we were able to draw on foreign professionals to help meet the manpower needs of the industry, while at the same time strengthen our local core.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: By working together, complementing each other more and competing with each other less, our Singapore workforce of "two-thirds local and one-third foreign" will be able to support a faster pace of industry transformation for us to compete better globally for better investments and jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan asked for flexibility for employers to hire foreign PMETs, especially those with skills in great shortage in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These include, for example, AI, data analytics, advanced manufacturing, digital services.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These are the expertise often cited in the media by various business groups.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Such professionals would command a salary premium and should be able to meet our EP criteria, in terms of salary, qualification and experience.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the exception of those on our FCF Watchlist, as long as the employing companies have complied with our FCF in giving fair consideration to our local PMETs, they should generally be able to obtain approval for work pass applications for such specialists in short supply globally and in critical shortage locally.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the exceptional situation where the EP applicants with the skillsets much needed here and yet are not able to meet our EP criteria, we do allow sector agencies to exercise some flexibility but only in a highly selective manner, on the condition that there is, indeed, a shortage of such skills here and that these foreign professionals are needed to help speed up our industry transformation and growth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is designed to improve the quality of both our local and foreign workforces in Singapore and enhance the complementarity with each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is so that we can meet the manpower needs of businesses for them to transform and grow and the career aspirations of our people for them to adapt and grow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Guided by this policy objective, we will introduce further changes to make "one-third foreign" even better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the S Pass holders who are mid-level skilled foreigners, their minimum qualifying salary was last updated in 2013.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As per current practice, those with more years of experience will need to meet higher salary thresholds.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will also provide a transition period for existing S Pass holders.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For Work Permit holders, there will be no further tightening for now, hence, no change to dependency ratio ceiling (DRC) and levy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As pointed out by Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Thomas Chua, our focus is to enhance the quality and productivity of these foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Work Permit holders at basic skill level (R2) from non-traditional sources and the People's Republic of China (PRC), they are now allowed to work here for a maximum of 10 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Those with higher skills (R1) in Services and Manufacturing are allowed to stay here for up to 18 years, and 22 years if they work in Construction, Process and Marine Shipyard.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, for those on 10 years, will now go to 14 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will also give employers more pathways to improve the quality of their foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Besides skills certification, those who are more experienced with higher salary can also be upgraded from R2 to R1 pass.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is currently allowed for Construction, Process and Services sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will now extend it to Manufacturing and Marine Shipyard sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe this will be helpful to companies that want to hire and retain their better Work Permit holders.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It will take effect from 1 September this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Fourth, for "two-thirds plus one-third, greater than one", we need to make the "plus" better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To recognise and spread the adoption of progressive HR practices, we launched the Human Capital Partnership (HCP) Programme in February last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are from various sectors ranging from MNCs to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay, Ms Jessica Tan and Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim asked for an update on HCP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, they have strong local core at all levels.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Collectively, local PMETs account for about 90% of the total PMET workforce in these companies; not just more than 90% at the entry to middle level, but also more than 80% at the senior to top levels.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Jobs are redesigned to be less physically demanding for the older workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: FWAs are offered to allow those with care responsibility at home to share job; and for employees to go on sabbaticals and pursue new opportunities within the company when they return; to pursue part-time studies to upgrade themselves; or to enable retired employees to return to work on a part-time basis.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Third, HCP companies believe strongly in strengthening local-foreign complementarity.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They transfer skills from foreign experts to our local workforce and build up the local core in their senior management team.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One HC Partner which left a deep impression on me is Keystone Cable.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Keystone Cable is a local SME with 140 employees.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is a maker of power and control cables with a strong foothold in the region.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The plant is located in Senoko, not easy to attract locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, it has to work doubly hard to compete with MNCs for talent.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But as a flexible and nimble SME, it embraces the mindset of human capital development.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He is now being groomed to take on clients in overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will also promote adoption of tripartite standards, as reminded by Ms Thanaletchimi.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Globally, there is big concern that technology will take away many jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Yet, we see an amazing race to embrace technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: China is the world’s No 1 user of industrial robots today.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Globally, there is a big concern that foreigners will take away jobs from the locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Yet, more countries are opening up even more to attract foreigners with the skills and expertise to offer, including China and Japan.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This reminded me of the story of two men walking in the jungle.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: One of them squatted down to tighten his shoelace, the other asked "what are you trying to do?" He said, "I am tightening the shoelace". "But the tiger is coming on us, you still have time to tighten your shoelace?" He said, "Yeah, because I am getting ready to run." "You mean you can run faster than a tiger?" "No, of course not.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But all I need to do is outrun you." Now, in the global village, it is not possible to outrun technology, but we can outrun the competition.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Those running slower will see more jobs being destroyed by technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Those who run faster can create new jobs with technology more than the loss of existing jobs to technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This explains why China is running fast with robots, and Japan is not slow, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the help of robots and AI, Honda Motor, Canon and Pioneer are bringing production of car components, car navigation systems, digital cameras back to Japan.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, "Made-in-Japan” is making a comeback but, this time, with the help of not just robots, but intelligent robots and human co-workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With the world out there running fast, just imagine, what if one day, a "cheaper" China becomes better by using technology faster than us, and a "better" Japan becomes cheaper also by using technology faster than us.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If this happens, they would become cheaper, better and faster than Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, the faster, the better, and we are.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At Bedok Industrial Estate, my constituency, Panasonic is building a Smart Factory there.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It will have machines fitted with sensors interconnected to work with one another.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Operations will be more manpower-lean and the local workers will be retrained to take on new and better jobs, such as robot coordinators.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We also have the AI Business Partnership Programme to encourage and facilitate AI adoption in our industry, and the AI Apprenticeship Programme to develop AI professionals with key skills, such as machine learning and deep learning.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In digital services, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is promoting fintech to realise our vision of becoming a Smart Financial Centre.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is working with industry to push through ground-breaking initiatives – blockchain, quantum computing, Big Data, AI and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, we move so fast that, today, Singapore is one of the top global fintech hubs alongside London, New York and Silicon Valley.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are also running fast in becoming a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the 1980s, when I was still a young man, we became an Intelligent Island through national computerisation, office automation and computer-integrated manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This time round, we aspire to become a Smart Nation and a Digital Government through the Internet-of-Things (IoT), National Digital Identity, Smart Urban Mobility, Cybersecurity and more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, to truly succeed in becoming a pervasively innovative economy and society, we need to do much more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We need to speed up the development and transfer of new and better global capabilities to our local workforce, a point made by Mr Chong Kee Hiong, not just in high-tech, high-profile and high-impact sectors, but in as many sectors as possible, and as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is why we are piloting CTP because the potential scope for transfer and development of new capabilities is limited only by our focus and determination.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In Precision Engineering, smartphones are getting bigger but flatter and lighter.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Hence, our local industry needs to use softer alloy and fit in more chips and components.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Companies need to use high-speed, high-precision machines to prevent cracking and warping.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Local engineers and technicians are also required to have new skills to advise on product design and material selection.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To compete well, our local industry needs to acquire new technologies and new capabilities to offer lower cost – to be cheaper; higher accuracy – to be better; and shorter cycle time – to be faster.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under CTP, over a period of 15 months, we support our precision engineering companies to install high-speed high-precision machines and to bring in foreign specialists from Germany to train our local trainers, training locally as well as through remote coaching, who are now able to train our local trainees from several companies in the industry.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To grow Singapore's market share in a global industry that is growing very fast, the Singapore Aircargo Agents Association (SAAA), the Changi Airport Group (CAG), the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) and the industry, they want to work together to bring in IATA-certified trainers from the UK and Dubai to train a group of local specialists here, who will then be able to multiply this capability by training other locals.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, here is another example of capability transfer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, in lift maintenance, the current approach is wait for the lift to break down, then repair, then wait for the lift to break down again.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A better approach actually is to make all our lifts in Singapore into "smart lifts", using predictive data analytics and maintenance, to shift from corrective maintenance, which means waiting for failure, to preventive maintenance before failure, which is being done by many companies today, to predictive maintenance, or reduce the probability of failure.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, predict what is likely to happen before it happens.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under CTP, we will partner leading global vendors to bring in overseas specialists or send our local trainers overseas so that, later on, they can return to train our local trainees here.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In this way, we can anchor "smart lift" capability in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Manufacturing facilities here focus mainly on made-to-order furniture.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, we can design and make furniture using three-axis Computer Numeric Control (CNC) machines.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I asked them what does it mean by "three-axis", they said these machines can move left, right, up, down, front and back.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the words of the industry themselves, we are now still at Industry 2.0.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To upgrade our local industry to 4.0, we will help them to bring in the 5-axis CNC machines where the tools can twist and turn, cut in different directions, to create contour and more complex shapes.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, this will also make the jobs of the craftsmen ESS!

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under CTP, the Singapore Furniture Industries Council, together with WSG, will bring in specialists from Italy to train our local trainers and craftsmen.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Another example of a domestic industry is car maintenance.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The market for hybrid cars grew by 200% in the last two years, from 6,000 a year to 20,000 last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: New capabilities are needed for the repair and maintenance of these hybrid cars, no longer just changing the oil filter, checking and replacing battery, lights and brakes, but have to handle a completely different system, such as carry out a battery load test, high voltage cable inspection, front motor test, hybrid transmission test and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Currently, independent third-party car workshops have no access to certifiable training to improve the skillsets of our local technicians.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under CTP, we will partner the Singapore Motor Workshop Association to bring in specialists from Germany to train our local mechanics and to transfer the capability to our local industry.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will support good projects from any company and any industry beyond those currently supported by economic agencies for specific sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for details of CTP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To achieve real transfer of capability, project duration is mostly in months and years, not days and weeks.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Specialists have to do more than just training but also coaching and working alongside our local workers and be their trainer, mentor and guide.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Costs can often be the obstacle, especially for local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under CTP, we will co-fund the cost of capability transfer for foreign specialists to train our locals here or for local trainers to be trained overseas so that, over time, we will be able to anchor more capabilities here to upgrade our local workforce and industries as we transform, adapt and grow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In reply to Mr Low Thia Khiang, I would like to assure him that in our project evaluation, we will consult the sector agencies and be guided by the various ITMs to ensure that these capabilities will really be relevant and able to strengthen our future competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about the funding levels.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Projects with higher impact on the industry and those benefiting SMEs will receive a higher level of support.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, Mr Low Thia Khiang would be pleased to hear this.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, if the industry impact benefits mainly SMEs, you will get a higher level of support.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Total funding per project is currently capped at $300,000.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Desmond Choo said we should scale up CTP and accelerate the acquisition of new capabilities.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We started the pilot late last year, just a few months ago.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will reach out extensively to create more awareness and generate more interest.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We hope our sector agencies and tripartite partners, including the Labour Movement and various industry groups, will make good use of CTP to fill the many capability gaps in a more pervasive manner.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We hope to do this across all sectors, with all sizes of companies, as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, if we work together, I am confident that even bad mathematics can be turned into good manpower policy for the benefit of all.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, the whole world is changing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In a world where only the fittest will survive, we have adopted a two-pronged strategy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, shi shi zao ying xiong (heroes are born out of circumstances).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The rapid development of technology and innovation is inevitable and cannot be stopped.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we refuse to make changes or are slow to adapt, we will definitely be eliminated.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: People say that it is better to suffer for the short term than to endure pain for the long term.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To continue with our development, we must master new technology, transform quickly and strengthen our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is something that we have achieved by working together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Economic transformation is like rowing a boat against the current.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we do not move forward, we will be pushed backwards.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our second strategy is ying xiong zao shi shi (heroes create the right circumstances for themselves).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we strengthen our economic competitiveness, we must also optimise our unique strengths and advantages, as well as strengthen the cohesiveness of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must ensure that the benefits and opportunities brought about by the future economy benefit every segment of our society, regardless of age, level of skills and income.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must pay special attention to older and lower-income workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must also help workers with young children and aged parents, so that they can look after their families while advancing their careers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We must also learn from others and overcome our shortcomings, ensure that locals and foreign workers can work better together and benefit from each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We should not be competing against each other within the country but against competitors overseas, in order to achieve better economic growth and better employment opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For some countries, just strengthening their economic competitiveness is considered a success but, for Singapore, we have to strengthen our competitiveness as well as the cohesiveness of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To us, that is what success really is about.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There are two types of pathways in this world: easy paths and difficult paths.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some countries choose the easy path because it is easier and they can travel faster, but eventually, instead of reaching their destination, they reach a dead end.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What we have chosen is not an easy path.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We know that in transformation and upgrading, there are no shortcuts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Although the path is not easy, but as long as our tripartite partners work together and help our workers, we will be able to move ahead of others.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When we reach the destination, it is definitely not a dead end but a brand-new wide horizon.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, let us continue to forge ahead together on this difficult path with a common belief, as one economy, as one society, as one country.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Only then can we ensure that Singapore continues to maintain a special place in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), in Asia and the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And only then can we ensure that our workers have better jobs, better wages, safe and happy homes, that each generation will be better than the last, and that lives continue to improve.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Together with our tripartite partners at the national and sector levels, we have to do our best to transform across all sectors, for our economy to transform and grow, pervasively, as One Singapore Unlimited.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We also have to do our best to create better jobs, better skills for everyone to adapt and grow inclusively as One Singapore United.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Together, we can strive for innovative, inclusive and sustainable growth for everyone.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ultimately, as Minister Heng Swee Keat said in Budget 2018: Together, A Better Future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I will be sharing what more MOM is doing to help Singaporeans have better jobs, better employment outcomes, better protection and better retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given that our workforce growth is slowing, our businesses have to become more manpower-lean.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, businesses may need to redesign jobs to support an ageing workforce or be more attractive to local jobseekers, who now have higher aspirations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM, together with several sector lead agencies, are helping businesses transform through LEDS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They come from all sectors and are of all sizes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One interesting project was undertaken by the Gratify Group, a company which owns many different food and beverage (F&B) brands.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The owner, Frank Lau, wanted to make sure that his company's expansion plans would not be held back as a result of a lack of manpower.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hence, when conceptualising its new brand which is called "Omoomodon", he set himself a challenge that every outlet must be able to operate with just three staff per shift, when most similar concepts needed at least five staff per shift.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the F&B business, what Frank wanted was certainly a tall order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But Frank believed that he needed to push the boundaries to have any chance of scaling the business in a sustainable way.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He engaged the Singapore Productivity Centre to redesign his workflow and processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They started with the menu, with food preparation very much in mind.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They studied operational flows at many food outlets and collected data on time-consuming tasks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The end result included a central kitchen, self-service ordering and payment and optimised kitchen designs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Staff were also crossed-trained to prepare food and attend to customers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The improved job scope resulted in better pay and higher retention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It provides a "one-stop" service for businesses, especially SMEs, to access schemes offered by different Government agencies, without having to figure out where and who to approach for what.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, not all transformations need customised solutions like Frank did.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many businesses will benefit just adopting ready-to-go productivity solutions, for example, the Smart Management and Tracking System (SMTS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Using radio frequency identification (RFID) technology to manage, track and audit assets to reduce stocktaking time, the companies can enjoy much productivity improvement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is useful for nearly all businesses in manufacturing and retail.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are now more than 40 ready-to-go solutions pre-approved by Government agencies, such as the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING) Singapore, the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These ready-to-go solutions have been tried and tested.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, there is no need for businesses to worry about ineffective solutions or fly-by-night vendors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Through LEDS, we aim to make technology and innovation pervasive, not only at the enterprise level, but also at the industry level, to quicken the pace of transformation, and not just in one or two sectors but across all 23 ITM sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For instance, under the Lean Hotel Initiative, 16 hotels came together to collectively identify gaps and design industry solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In just four months, the hotels had achieved productivity savings of between 4.5% and 28%, without having to compromise service quality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also plan to go beyond the ITMs to non-ITM sectors, and are in discussions with several industries, such as furniture, farms, lifts and escalators, to support their transformation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, as businesses transform and jobs become better, so, too, must workers adapt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is how we can achieve better employment outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Broadly speaking, we aim to help both missed matches − where employer and jobseekers have not found each other, and mismatches − where there are skills or wage gaps that make it hard for the jobseeker to secure a job.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Of the 25,000 jobseekers placed, about 60% involved missed matches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The jobseekers were job-ready but somehow missed finding the right employers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: WSG and NTUC-e2i helped them to find a match.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked for an update on our efforts to strengthen job matching through the national Jobs Bank.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are transforming Jobs Bank into a new platform called MyCareersFuture.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MyCareersFuture will have new features to help jobseekers and employers find better matches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will have intelligent job matching, and can recommend jobs to jobseekers that would best fit their skillsets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will also highlight jobs that are supported by Adapt and Grow programmes, such as PCPs, to help bridge job and skill mismatches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides reducing missed matches, we helped to close skills or wage mismatches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Of the 25,000 jobseekers placed, 40% involved jobseekers with some form of mismatch.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This proportion has grown significantly from just 25% in 2016.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This reflects our more intensive efforts to address mismatches.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As our economy restructures, job-skills mismatch will be a growing challenge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They can be very unsettling for individuals who have lost their jobs or are at risk of retrenchment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why our key focus has been to step up support for jobseekers with skills or wage mismatches, because they need more help.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, we strengthened support under PCP and CSP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim, Mr Low Thia Khiang and Dr Intan Mokhtar asked how effective MOM's efforts have been in helping the long-term unemployed, older workers and mature workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If Members recall, CSP provides a wage subsidy that helps to close the gap between what PMET jobseekers expect and what employers are prepared to offer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The retention rate of those placed has been encouraging.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides CSP, we also raised the salary support caps of PCPs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: PCP placements in 2017 were almost three times that in 2016.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In particular, the proportion of mature PMETs, especially those who are 50 years old and above, has more than doubled.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similarly, the proportion placed in mid-level jobs paying $4,000 or more has also doubled.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi would be happy to know that overall dropout rates for PCPs are low as more than nine in 10 participants complete the programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even in the healthcare sector which has a longer training period for PCPs, almost nine in 10 have successfully completed the programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For the minority who drop out, most have personal reasons, or find it challenging to adapt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have worked with the Ministry of Health (MOH) to reduce the duration of some PCPs, such as nursing, without compromising the quality of training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More importantly, we need to strike a balance between stringent criteria and processes to screen individuals and give jobseekers sufficient opportunities to start new careers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One person who has started a new career is Mr Soon Sie Chye who is 44 years old.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After graduating with a degree in Electronic and Electrical Engineering from Loughborough University, Sie Chye spent the early part of his career working as an engineer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More than 10 years ago, he made a career switch to join the banking sector, where he had a fruitful career, leading back office teams in different banks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, he always had a lifelong dream to set up his own business.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2014, he took the plunge but, in less than two years, the venture failed and he became unemployed for more than a year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It was a challenging and stressful period as he just had a newborn.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
